fetched_contents.text: Evaluating refractory material performance in pyrometallurgical recycling of lithium-ion batteries under a reducing atmosphere 1. Introduction In pursuing sustainable energy solutions, recycling lithium-ion batteries (LIB) has emerged as a critical process, particularly within the pyrometallurgical sector [1]. This method, favored for its robustness against varying input streams, is integral to recovering valuable metals from spent LIBs [2,3]. Alternative recycling routes for LIBs, such as hydro- and bio-hydrometallurgy, are often highly susceptible to a varying input stream. Therefore, only some are used as stand-alone recycling routes within the industry [4]. While in pyrometallurgical routes, the main focus is put on Nickel (Ni) and Cobalt (Co), due to their prevailing economic relevance, Lithium (Li) is most often being slagged and therefore economically lost [5]. With Li designated as a critical raw material by the European Union and establishment of a mandatory recycling quota of 80 % by 2031, the appeal of recycling Li has been significantly amplified [6]. This circumstance is further underscored by Li's fluctuating price dynamics, highlighting the strategic importance of securing its supply through recycling initiatives [7]. To address this impending concern, a pyrometallurgical recycling approach is being developed by the Chair of Thermal Processing Technologies at Montanuniversität Leoben, being able to circumvent the limitations encountered by currently used industrial recycling methods. The proposed process route with the InduRed reactor as the core principle is capable of recovering Li and Phosphorous (P) via the gaseous phase while simultaneously producing an alloy containing elements such as Ni, Co, Manganese (Mn), and Iron (Fe). The principle is based on the carbothermic reduction of the input material via an inductively heated packed bed [8]. Although the slagging of lithium has verifiably been shown to be suppressed, a significant unresolved issue is finding refractory materials that are stable against the highly aggressive components of LIBs [9]. Previous use of refractories, particularly aluminum oxide (Al2O3) [5,10] and magnesium oxide (MgO) [11], has exposed challenges in terms of corrosion mainly due to the formation of cobalt aluminates (CoAl2O4) [12,13] using Al2O3 as refractory material and lithium diffusion within the crucible walls using MgO [14]. Corrosion, generally defined as the chemical attack on refractory material by a liquid phase such as slag, metal or alloy, occurs when the melt infiltrates the refractory matrix, creating capillaries that weaken the material's mechanical strength [15]. During this process, the fine grain of the refractory is washed out leaving the coarse grain exposed. This process occurs due to the chemical reaction between the liquid slag and solid refractory phases. It continues until the saturation point of the slag or the metal bath occurs through the refractory material [16]. Such issues can lead to contamination of the input material and significantly impact refractory stability and reusability. Furthermore, diffusion-related constraints can hinder lithium removal rates, thereby diminishing the overall process efficiency [17]. The challenge in pyrometallurgical recycling of LIBs lies in identifying refractory materials that withstand aggressive conditions at high temperatures and minimize the diffusion and corrosion caused by the complex mix of materials in spent batteries. This statement can be supported by findings from Qu et al. [18], where pyrometallurgical recycling of LIB with MgO and Al2O3 refractory materials showed severe dissolution effects of the crucible materials in the alloy, leading to increased dynamic viscosities and ultimately decreased metal recovery rates [18]. Per definition, refractories are non-metallic ceramic materials capable of withstanding temperatures higher than 1500 °C per DIN 51 060, where the refractoriness is defined by the pyrometric cone equivalent [19]. Most modern refractories are based on one or more non-metallic oxides, which can be divided into basic and non-basic refractories. All basic products are based on either calcium oxide (CaO) or MgO, whereas non-basic materials are based on Al2O3, silicon dioxide (SiO2) or zirconium oxide (ZrO2) [20]. This is a fundamental differentiation, as the correct refractory material is often based on the basicity of the medium in contact with the lining. In the case of the InduRed Reactor, this is mainly a molten phase consisting of elements such as Co, Ni and Fe and a gaseous phase containing Li, P and carbon monoxide (CO) [21]. Especially the highly reductive CO atmosphere present within the InduRed must be considered, as CO can react with FeO in the lining material. The reaction leads to carbon production, which sits within the refractory structure, leading to a loss in mechanical strength and increased cracking [22]. This reaction can occur at iron contents below 0,1 wt% metallic Fe [21]. Furthermore, refractories are differentiated into shaped and unshaped products. Shaped products are generally defined as all products delivered with a predefined geometry, where the most common forms are bricks [23]. Unshaped products, also known as monolithics, contain a wide range of products such as plastics, ramming mixes, mortars and castables, using either a chemical or hydraulic bond. The materials used in this paper are all hydraulic bonded castables with hydraulic bonds, which are then shaped using vibration [23] The hydraulic bond gives a mechanical strength up to temperatures of approximately 600 °C. After that, a ceramic bond is necessary, achieved by firing the mixes at temperatures between 1200 °C and 1500 °C. The achieved ceramic bond allows a temperature resistance of up to 1800 °C depending on the used raw material [21]. fetched_contents.text: Automation on thermal control of blast furnace 1. Introduction Blast furnaces produce hot metal from raw materials such as sintered iron ore and coke and are still operated manually by skilled operators. Low production costs and CO2 emissions require a reduction of the reducing agent ratio (RAR), which makes it more difficult to operate the furnace in a stable manner. Precise control of the furnace state through process automation is the key to realizing efficient and stable operation (Iffat et al., 2018; Sprin et al., 2021; Rybolovlev et al., 2015). In the blast furnace, it is crucial to maintain a constant temperature of hot metal drained from the furnace bottom. If the hot metal temperature (HMT) becomes too low, the hot metal and its byproduct, i.e., slag, solidify in the furnace, and it may lead to shut-down. On the other hand, an excessively high HMT results in an excess consumption of the reducing agent. Maintaining the HMT at a lower bound with small variations would allow both the reduction of RAR and a stable operation. The slow and complex process dynamics of the blast furnaces makes HMT control difficult. Although operators adjust manipulated variables based on future predictions of the HMT, it is difficult to accurately predict the effects of previous control actions on the future HMT due to the large time constant of more than eight hours, and the control actions tend to be excessive. As a result, the deviation of HMT from its set point becomes too large, which is a common issue in manual operations (Hashimoto et al., 2019a). In addition, the same problem occurs when we use classical control methods such as PID control due to the large time constant and dead time. Numerous methods have been proposed to control HMT and the Si content in the hot metal, which are the indicators of the heat level in a blast furnace. Jiang et al. developed an operation guidance system to maintain a constant Si content using a recurrent neural network based on feature selection (Jiang et al., 2020). Azadi et al. achieved an accurate prediction of the Si content by using a hybrid model combining first principles and data-based models (Azadi et al., 2022a, 2022b). Agrawal et al. developed a proactive thermal indicator based on the energy balance for controlling HMT (Agrawal et al., 2019). We developed a two-dimensional (2D) transient model of the blast furnace (Hashimoto et al., 2019b), and achieved the accurate prediction of the eight-hour-ahead HMT by embedding moving horizon estimation (MHE) (Hashimoto et al., 2019c). We also implemented an operation guidance system to control HMT by non-linear model predictive control (NMPC) in real plants (Hashimoto et al., 2019b). However, these conventional technologies are all limited to be used in operation guidance systems, which present the recommended control actions to human operators. In this study, we developed a control system to realize the full automation of HMT control and verified its control performance in an actual plant. The selection of appropriate manipulated variables is an issue for controlling HMT. The HMT can be controlled by manipulating the pulverized coal ratio (PCR), which is the amount of pulverized coal per ton of hot metal, the coke ratio (CR), the blast moisture (BM), and the blast temperature (BT). There are practical restrictions on most of these manipulated variables, however. CR is rarely actively manipulated to control HMT to reduce operation costs. The BM should be kept near the lower limit since the addition of moisture requires an excess amount of reducing agent to compensate for heat absorption by the decomposition of water vapor. In recent years, the BT has been kept at the upper limit in an attempt to reduce RAR. Since CR, BM, and BT are less suitable for use as manipulated variables, PCR was selected as the manipulated variable in the developed control system. In this study, a cascade control system was constructed as shown in Fig. 1, which consists of an outer HMT control loop and an inner PCR tracking control loop. The HMT controller calculates the target PCR based on the future prediction of HMT, and the PCR tracking controller calculates the pulverized coal (PC) flow rate using the predicted PCR. Both future HMT and PCR are predicted by the 2D transient model considering the effect of disturbances such as coke ratio and blast volume. The period of calculating the control actions of the target PCR and PC flow rate is 15 min. We also developed a closed-loop control system that automatically (or semi-automatically, requiring the operator's approval) executes the control actions. We finally evaluated the control accuracy of HMT in the real plant. The outline of this paper is as follows. Section 2 explains the algorithms of the HMT control and the PCR tracking control and the implementation method of these control algorithms. Section 3 describes the optimization results of target PCR and PC flow rate by the HMT control and PCR control, respectively, and demonstrates the control performance of the developed control system in the real plant. Finally, Section 4 concludes the paper. 2. Methodology This section describes the 2D transient model used in the developed control system, the method of calculating the optimal target PCR for HMT control, and the method of calculating the optimal PC flow rate for PCR tracking control. The implementation method of HMT control and PCR tracking control in a real plant is also presented. 2.1. 2D transient model Various blast furnace models have been developed (Abhale et al., 2020), including one-dimensional (1D) transient models (Hashimoto et al., 2019a; Saxén, 1990), 2D steady-state models (Fu et al., 2014), 2D transient models (Hashimoto et al., 2018; Castro et al., 2000), and three-dimensional (3D) transient models (Shen et al., 2016; Jiao et al., 2020). Recent furnace design changes have improved energy efficiency through a combination of shape, refractory, heat-recovery, and automation-related improvements, with each change targeting specific operational losses and inefficiencies. The evidence points to several concrete design elements and mechanisms.

First, refractory lining improvements are a major efficiency driver. The refractory evidence emphasizes that refractory materials must withstand extreme temperatures and resist corrosion and diffusion under aggressive conditions. In pyrometallurgical recycling of lithium-ion batteries, refractory materials are exposed to slag and alloy infiltration, which can weaken mechanical strength and reduce process efficiency [N2-F2]. The same source notes that advanced refractory materials offer better thermal efficiency and can reduce heat-up and cool-down times, improving furnace savings [N2-R3]. While the evidence is strongest for refractory performance in recycling, it still supports the broader point that better refractory lining reduces thermal losses and extends furnace life, thereby lowering energy demands and downtime costs [N2-R2][N2-F2].

Second, heat-recovery integration is explicitly identified as a key efficiency feature. Hatch’s furnace solutions include “proprietary heat recovery technology” and “complete systems to valorize slags and provide opportunities for energy efficiency” [N6-F4]. The waste heat recovery evidence also frames this as a broad industrial process improvement, with a comprehensive review of methodologies and state-of-the-art technologies [N7-R1]. Combined with Hatch’s mention of air-water granulation and heat recovery systems [N7-R3], the evidence suggests that furnace modifications now routinely incorporate heat recovery to capture waste heat from exhaust gases, slag valorization, and off-gas systems. This reduces fuel consumption by reusing otherwise lost thermal energy, rather than treating the furnace as a heat sink [N6-F4][N7-R1].

Third, furnace shape and feed-system design changes are implied by the evidence on furnace feed systems and refractory design. Hatch’s page describes “customized feed systems designed for precise material handling and optimized thermal performance” and “tailored rectangular and circular refractory designs engineered for high-intensity smelting and unique process challenges” [N6-F4]. While the evidence does not spell out every shape change in detail, it does show that furnace geometry and feed handling are being redesigned to improve thermal performance and process control. This likely reduces fuel consumption by minimizing uneven heating, slag accumulation, and inefficient material flow, which in turn lowers the need for excessive energy input to maintain temperature [N6-F4].

Fourth, automation and process-control improvements are central to energy efficiency. The process-control evidence shows that automation is used to achieve efficient and stable furnace operation, and that control systems are used to maintain constant temperature and reduce reducing-agent usage [N3-F3]. Specifically, the blast-furnace automation study explains that precise thermal control is needed because slow process dynamics make manual operation difficult, and that automation can reduce reducing agent ratio (RAR), lower fuel use, and stabilize operation [N3-F3]. The broader pyrometallurgical-control evidence also states that “implementing advanced process control systems is essential for optimizing pyrometallurgical operations” [N3-R4]. This suggests that furnace modifications are not only hardware-based but also increasingly software- and control-based, with automation reducing energy waste from unstable operation and excessive adjustments [N3-R2][N3-F3].

The operational conditions most affected by these changes are temperature regulation, reducing-agent use, and thermal cycling. Refractory and heat-recovery changes affect high-temperature durability and heat loss [N2-F2][N7-R1]. Process-control and automation changes affect temperature stability, RAR, and the need for frequent adjustments [N3-F3]. Heat-recovery integration also affects slag valorization and off-gas handling, because waste heat recovery is tied to exhaust and slag systems [N6-F4]. Together, these design elements reduce fuel consumption by improving thermal retention, lowering auxiliary heating needs, and stabilizing process conditions so that less energy is wasted in overshooting or correcting temperature deviations [N2-F2][N3-F3][N7-R1].

Overall, the evidence supports a pattern in which furnace design changes improve energy efficiency by reducing thermal losses through better insulation/refractories, capturing waste heat, and stabilizing operation through automation [N2-F2][N6-F4][N3-F3]. The strongest evidence is not a single universal design template, but rather a set of complementary changes: refractory improvement, heat recovery, optimized feed systems, and automation-driven thermal control [N2-F2][N6-F4][N3-F3][N7-R1].

Recent furnace modifications have improved product recovery and selectivity by targeting slag handling, gas-flow optimization, and process control, with evidence pointing to better recovery of metals, reduced impurity carryover, and improved separation of byproducts. The key products or byproducts improved include metals from slags, valuable metals from industrial waste streams, and slag itself, while the evidence on selectivity is strongest in the context of copper processing, pyrometallurgical slag valorization, and metal recovery from waste materials.

On product recovery, the evidence indicates that pyrometallurgical processes are being used to recover valuable metals from slags and industrial waste streams. For example, a review on pyrometallurgical processing of ferrous slag describes slag as a “co-product” and notes that slag treatment can be part of a zero-waste approach [N5-R1]. Another review summarizes various extraction methods including pyrometallurgical methods for recovering precious metals from steel industry slag [N5-R2]. A separate review describes pyrometallurgical methods involving roasting and selective reduction for precious metal recovery [N5-R3]. This suggests that furnace modifications are increasingly designed to recover metals from slag and byproduct streams rather than simply producing molten metal, thereby improving metal recovery from materials that were previously discarded [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3].

The evidence also points to improved selectivity through slag treatment and separation. The same review on ferrous slag notes that slag is conventionally quenched with pressurized water or cooled on the cooling yard, and that pyrometallurgical processing can be part of a zero-waste strategy [N5-R1]. Another review on nickel smelting slag modification states that slag can be modified by reduction and sulfurization to make it more amenable to metal recovery through flotation [N5-R4]. This implies that furnace design and process changes are improving the separation of metals from slag by making the slag more workable and less contaminated, which in turn increases selectivity and recovery [N5-R4]. The broader pyrometallurgy overview also states that metal recovery can be improved by choosing a proper slag system and recovering target metals from slag via hydrometallurgy [N6-R2]. Although the evidence is strongest for slag-based recovery, it supports the broader conclusion that furnace modifications can improve recovery by optimizing slag composition and handling [N6-R2][N5-R4].

Gas-flow and combustion optimization also affect metal recovery, particularly in copper pyrometallurgy. The combustion-optimization evidence notes that efficiency can vary with furnace design, load, excess air, flue-gas temperature, and furnace conditions, and that adjusting residual O2 concentration, air preheat temperature, and damper angle can improve furnace burning efficiency [N4-R1][N4-R2]. The industrial-gas chapter on copper pyrometallurgy emphasizes the use of industrial gases to achieve increased productivity and sustainability, suggesting that optimized gas flow can support more efficient melting and better control of metal recovery [N4-R4]. The high-accuracy simulation evidence also shows that pyrometallurgical processes involve multicomponent gas phases and molten phases, which implies that gas-flow changes can influence how metal and slag move within the furnace and how reactions proceed [N4-R3]. This means that process-control and gas-flow changes can improve recovery by reducing carryover, improving reaction completeness, and better separating metal from slag [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4].

Evidence on reduced impurity carryover or slag loss is indirect but still present. The slag-value evidence notes that slag is a byproduct that can be treated to extract valuable metals [N5-R1], implying that improvements in slag handling can reduce loss. The refractory evidence also indicates that corrosion and diffusion can contaminate input material and reduce process efficiency [N2-F2], which is relevant to impurity carryover because refractory failure can introduce contaminants into the melt. The automation evidence adds that precise process control helps maintain stable operation and reduce variability, which can minimize carryover of uncontrolled material from one phase to another [N3-F3]. Together, these sources suggest that furnace modifications can reduce impurity carryover by improving slag separation, minimizing contamination from refractories, and stabilizing process conditions [N5-R1][N2-F2][N3-F3].

In summary, the evidence shows that furnace modifications improve product recovery and selectivity by better recovering metals from slags and waste streams, improving slag handling and separation, and optimizing gas-flow and combustion conditions [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R4][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4]. The strongest evidence is for metal recovery from slags and slag valorization, but there is also support for reduced impurity carryover through process control and better refractory performance [N2-F2][N3-F3].

Adopting new furnace technologies faces economic and practical barriers, including capital costs, retrofitting challenges, and downtime implications, while the benefits must be weighed against current operating constraints and the conditions under which upgrades are most cost-effective.

Capital costs are a clear barrier. The evidence does not provide a direct cost-figure table, but it does show that furnace modifications are often part of larger system upgrades, such as proprietary heat recovery technology, customized feed systems, and advanced monitoring and control systems [N6-F4]. This implies that retrofitting is not a simple plug-and-play change, but a system-level investment. The automation evidence also emphasizes that control systems are used in real plants but require implementation and optimization [N3-F3]. Because furnace upgrades often involve process-control, refractory, feed, and heat-recovery components, the upfront capital cost is likely substantial, especially for older or non-modular facilities [N6-F4][N3-F3].

Retrofitting challenges are supported by the evidence on refractory and furnace-design changes. Refractory performance must be compatible with extreme temperatures and aggressive process conditions, and refractory failure can reduce efficiency and process stability [N2-F2]. This suggests that retrofitting must account for not only the physical replacement of linings but also the broader furnace geometry, feed handling, and thermal performance [N2-F2][N6-F4]. The process-control evidence also notes that blast-furnace automation requires precise prediction and control because of slow process dynamics and large time constants [N3-F3]. Retrofitting automation systems would therefore require not only software changes but also integration with existing sensors, models, and plant infrastructure, which can complicate implementation [N3-F3]. Overall, retrofitting is a complex and disruptive task that may require partial or full redesign of furnace subsystems [N6-F4][N3-F3].

Downtime implications are also significant. The refractory evidence states that refractory corrosion and diffusion can reduce mechanical strength and process efficiency [N2-F2]. In a production setting, this could necessitate unplanned shutdowns or reduced throughput while refractories are replaced or repaired. The automation evidence notes that the blast-furnace control system requires careful implementation and verification in real plants, with a closed-loop control system that can be fully automated or semi-automated [N3-F3]. This implies that downtime can be reduced if automation is implemented correctly, but the initial commissioning and validation period may still involve operational disruption. The waste heat recovery evidence also frames heat recovery as a state-of-the-art technology, which suggests that retrofitting heat-recovery systems may require temporary modifications or additional infrastructure that can delay startup [N7-R1][N6-F4].

The benefits of upgrades must be compared with current operating constraints. The automation evidence shows that precise thermal control is essential because manual operation is error-prone and inefficient [N3-F3]. This implies that the operating constraint of unstable temperature and reducing-agent use is a strong incentive for automation. The heat-recovery evidence also shows that waste heat recovery can improve energy efficiency [N7-R1][N6-F4], which is valuable when energy costs or carbon constraints are tight. However, the evidence also shows that these benefits are conditional on process dynamics, refractory compatibility, and system integration [N3-F3][N2-F2]. In other words, the benefit of an upgrade depends on whether the furnace can be redesigned or retrofitted to support it, rather than on the upgrade itself alone.

Guidance on when upgrades are most cost-effective is indirect but still present. The automation evidence suggests that upgrades are most valuable when they can reduce RAR, stabilize operation, and improve predictability, especially in large, slow-process systems [N3-F3]. The heat-recovery evidence implies that upgrades are cost-effective when waste heat can be captured and reused, and when slag valorization can be integrated [N7-R1][N6-F4]. The refractory evidence suggests that upgrades are most cost-effective when refractory failure is frequent or severe, because better refractories can reduce downtime, extend asset life, and lower replacement costs [N2-F2]. Taken together, the evidence points to cost-effectiveness when upgrades address a material operational constraint—such as unstable temperature, excessive fuel use, or frequent refractory failure—and when the plant has the capacity to retrofit the necessary subsystems [N3-F3][N7-R1][N2-F2].

In conclusion, the economic and practical barriers to adopting new furnace technologies include high capital costs, complex retrofitting, and potential downtime during implementation [N6-F4][N3-F3][N2-F2]. The benefits are most valuable when they reduce fuel use, stabilize operation, improve energy recovery, and extend equipment life, making upgrades most cost-effective in plants where process instability, refractory degradation, or energy inefficiency is significant [N3-F3][N7-R1][N2-F2].

## Integrated final answer: how recent technological modifications in pyrometallurgical furnaces have enhanced energy efficiency and product recovery

Recent technological modifications in pyrometallurgical furnaces have improved both energy efficiency and product recovery by combining furnace-design, materials, process-control, gas-flow, and heat-recovery innovations. The evidence points to a broad pattern: newer furnaces are not only more thermally efficient, but also better at capturing and separating valuable metals from slags and waste streams, with automation and simulation enabling more precise control of complex processes.

### 1) Energy-efficiency improvements from furnace design changes

Recent design changes have improved energy efficiency through several complementary mechanisms, with the strongest evidence supporting refractory performance, heat recovery, and automation-driven thermal control.

#### a) Refractory and insulation improvements reduce thermal losses
A key efficiency driver is the refractory lining. The evidence shows that refractory materials must withstand extreme temperatures and resist corrosion and diffusion under aggressive conditions, because refractory failure can weaken mechanical strength and reduce process efficiency [N2-F2]. Advanced refractory materials are also described as improving thermal efficiency and reducing heat-up and cool-down times, which directly lowers energy demand and downtime [N2-R3]. While the evidence is strongest in the context of pyrometallurgical recycling of lithium-ion batteries, it still supports the broader conclusion that better refractory design reduces heat loss and improves furnace durability [N2-F2][N2-R2].

#### b) Heat-recovery integration captures waste energy
Heat-recovery technology is another major efficiency gain. Hatch’s furnace solutions explicitly mention proprietary heat recovery technology and systems to valorize slags for energy efficiency [N6-F4].
